Uniform baseline hyperparameters without documented method-specific tuning also make collapsed VDE results insufficient evidence that prior approaches cannot scale to proteins.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the extensive appendix. The physical training lag, construction of lagged pairs after random frame subsampling, conditioning-network specification, and key optimization settings are insufficiently documented. The code-availability statement is unfinished. These omissions concern the central algorithm rather than peripheral implementation choices.

Claims of scalability and a comprehensive benchmark exceed the demonstrated scope. The main study covers three small proteins using samples from long trajectories that already contain folding events. Performance with limited trajectory data, broader protein diversity, and larger systems is untested, and overlap with BioEmu's pretraining data is not characterized.

strengths: Conditioning a frozen BioEmu model on a learned CV to predict future conformations is a promising approach. Deploying only the compact encoder during enhanced sampling is practically attractive.

The experimental effort is substantial: explicit-solvent OPES and steered MD on three proteins, comparisons using shared training data and descriptors, structural analyses, and several component ablations.
The combined CV-and-RMSD steering protocol produces strong results on Chignolin and BBA: target-hit rates reach 100% and 93.8%, versus 43.8% and 18.8% for the best reported baselines.
The appendices provide useful additional evidence, including VAMP scores, an alanine-dipeptide extension, and informative negative results from steering without RMSD.
weaknesses: The main steering results do not isolate the learned CV's contribution. Appendix B.4 specifies a composite coordinate combining the learned CV with target RMSD. Without RMSD, BIOEMU-CV achieves only 0–6.2% target hits on Chignolin and 0% on Trp-cage and BBA under the tested settings (Table 15). An RMSD-only baseline is essential to establish the incremental benefit. This dependency also needs clear disclosure in the main experimental description.

The free-energy comparison uses inconsistent physical observables across methods. Folded and unfolded basins are defined by bisecting each model's CV range, producing different reference folding free energies, sometimes with opposite signs. For BBA, the references are 2.76 for DeepTICA and -2.88 for TAE. These comparisons need a shared structural state definition and consistently reweighted populations; marking selected results N/A does not resolve the issue.

The statistical treatment weakens the OPES conclusions. The most deviant of four runs is discarded for Trp-cage and BBA, although trapping is itself relevant sampling performance. Reporting the absolute error of the average can also conceal cancellation between inaccurate runs. All-run results, per-run errors, and uncertainty on improvements are needed. BIOEMU-CV's BBA estimate remains 9.99 versus a reference of 2.77, so accurate convergence is not established.

The specific benefits of foundation-model pretraining and time-lagged conditioning are insufficiently isolated. There is no comparable generative-model control without BioEmu pretraining on the protein tasks. The Chignolin ablation is also mixed: removing time-lagged conditioning improves PMF MAE from 3.07 to 1.41 (Table 13), despite the text claiming improvement across downstream tasks. Broader, consistently interpreted ablations are needed.

Evidence for capturing slow dynamics and scaling remains limited. State discrimination and successful driven endpoints do not establish dynamical fidelity. VAMP scores are competitive rather than consistently superior, and the Chignolin committor correlation trails VDE. The protein experiments cover only three small systems and use frames from long equilibrium trajectories, leaving effectiveness with limited trajectory data or larger proteins unresolved.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite detailed simulation settings. The physical training lag, construction of time-lagged pairs after frame subsampling, and conditioning-adapter configuration are insufficiently specified. Appendix B.2 lists a 45-input architecture despite larger descriptor dimensions for the other proteins. The reproducibility statement ends with an unfinished resource reference and supplies no usable code link.

strengths: Conditioning a frozen BioEmu model through a learned low-dimensional encoder is a plausible and useful approach to transferring generative-model knowledge into collective-variable learning.
The evaluation includes substantial explicit-solvent simulations on three miniproteins, multiple established baselines, structural analyses, and useful component ablations.

Within the reported RMSD-assisted steering setup, BIOEMU-CV achieves substantial gains on Chignolin and BBA: target-hit rates of 100% and 93.8%, versus baseline bests of 43.8% and 18.8%, respectively.
weaknesses: The main steering results do not isolate the learned CV’s contribution. Appendix B.4 reveals that steering uses f_theta(x) minus target RMSD. Without RMSD assistance, Table 15 reports only 0–6.2% success for BIOEMU-CV on Chignolin and 0% on the other proteins under the tested settings. Although all methods receive this assistance, an RMSD-only baseline is essential to establish the additional value of the learned representation. This dependence should also be explicit in the main results.

The folding free-energy comparison lacks a common physical definition of the states. Each method divides its own CV range in half, producing different reference quantities for the same protein; for example, Trp-cage has reference values of -1.45 for TAE and 4.15 for BIOEMU-CV. Agreement with these different targets does not establish comparable accuracy in physical folding free energy. All methods should be evaluated using shared structural basin definitions and consistent reweighting.

The statistical treatment weakens the convergence evidence. Appendix B.3 removes the most deviant of four runs for Trp-cage and BBA, even though trapping is a relevant failure of enhanced sampling. Reporting the absolute error of the mean can also conceal errors that cancel across runs. Uncertainty remains substantial: BIOEMU-CV’s BBA estimate is 9.99 ± 5.43 against a reference of 2.77. Results including every run and uncertainty on comparative errors are needed.

The ablations do not convincingly establish the proposed mechanism or the importance of foundation-model pretraining. Freezing versus unfreezing pretrained BioEmu does not replace a matched comparison without pretraining. Moreover, Table 13’s non-time-lagged variant has better PMF MAE than the proposed method, 1.41 versus 3.07, contradicting the accompanying claim of uniformly improved downstream performance. The Chignolin committor correlation and VAMP results also show no consistent advantage.

Baseline failures are insufficiently diagnosed. Using identical dropout and an absolute early-stopping threshold across differently scaled objectives is not evidence of adequate tuning. The collapsed VDE representations warrant further investigation before attributing failure to protein size. PCA/TICA comparisons are limited to Trp-cage steering, and physical CV baselines such as native contacts are missing from the main benchmark.

Target-reaching under strong, short-duration steering is insufficient evidence of physically representative transition paths. Maximum potential energy over successful trajectories and projections onto two TICA coordinates do not validate the transition-path distribution or kinetic fidelity. The path-sampling conclusions should be narrowed or supported by additional dynamical validation.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the lengthy appendix. The protein-training lag in physical units, construction of time-lagged pairs from randomly sampled frames, and important optimization and adapter details are not adequately specified. Appendix B.2 gives a 45-input architecture for all proteins despite reporting 190 and 378 input distances for the larger systems. The reproducibility statement also ends with an unfinished code-resource sentence.

The broad scalability and benchmark claims exceed the demonstrated scope. The main evidence covers three small proteins and training samples drawn from long trajectories already containing folding events. There is no convincing assessment of reduced trajectory requirements or substantially larger systems, and the positioning understates earlier protein applications of learned CV methods.

strengths: The proposed use of time-lagged conditioning on a frozen BioEmu model is a plausible and useful approach to learning compact collective variables, with a small encoder used during simulation.
The study includes substantial explicit-solvent simulation work on three proteins, comparisons with established time-lagged methods, and complementary structural and dynamical diagnostics.
The combined learned-CV/RMSD steering results are promising: BIOEMU-CV achieves 100% target hits on Chignolin and 93.8% on BBA, substantially exceeding the reported baselines.
The appendix provides useful ablations of time-lagged conditioning, backbone freezing, encoder size, conditioning placement, and RMSD mixing, including disclosure of unsuccessful configurations.
weaknesses: The strongest transition-path results depend on a major confound. Appendix B.4 reveals that steering uses the learned CV combined with target RMSD, rather than the learned CV alone. Without RMSD, BIOEMU-CV achieves only 0–6.2% target hits in Table 15. An RMSD-only baseline is missing, so the added value over direct structural steering remains unestablished. This dependence should be explicit in the main results.

The free-energy benchmark does not use common physical state definitions across methods. Dividing each learned CV range in half produces different reference folding free energies, including opposite signs for Trp-cage: -1.45 for TAE versus 4.15 for BIOEMU-CV. These are different thermodynamic quantities, weakening direct comparisons. Evaluation should use shared structural basin definitions and consistently reweighted observables.

The statistical treatment weakens the OPES evidence. For Trp-cage and BBA, the run farthest from the four-run mean is discarded, although trapping is itself an important sampling failure. Reporting the absolute error of the averaged estimate can also conceal cancellation between inaccurate runs. Variability remains large, and BIOEMU-CV's BBA free-energy error is still 7.22 kJ/mol. All-run results and uncertainty on comparative performance are needed.

The evidence that time-lagged conditioning specifically improves slow-mode recovery is mixed. In Table 13, removing the time lag improves PMF MAE from 3.07 to 1.41, despite the accompanying claim of improvement on both downstream tasks. Committor correlations and VAMP scores also show no consistent superiority. Lag-sensitivity experiments and appropriate held-out dynamical validation would strengthen the central interpretation.

The contribution of foundation-model pretraining is insufficiently isolated. Freezing versus fine-tuning does not establish the benefit of pretrained BioEmu over a matched generative model trained without those weights. The alanine experiment uses a different backbone and an additional autocorrelation loss, so it does not resolve this attribution.

Claims of comprehensive benchmarking and scalability exceed the demonstrated scope. The protein experiments cover three small systems with substantial existing equilibrium trajectories. Baseline tuning is insufficiently justified: identical dropout and early-stopping thresholds across differently scaled objectives need not provide comparable optimization. Failures of these configurations do not establish that existing methods generally cannot handle proteins.

Reproduction is materially hindered by missing training details, including the actual training lag in physical units, construction of time-lagged pairs from the sampled frames, and complete adapter and optimization settings. The reproducibility statement ends with an unfinished resource reference. Furthermore, endpoint RMSD and maximum potential energy along successful steered paths provide limited validation of physically representative transition pathways.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: learning useful collective variables for molecular simulation. Conditioning a frozen BioEmu model through a compact encoder is a plausible and potentially useful approach.

The experimental effort is substantial, including explicit-solvent simulations on three proteins, comparisons with three learned-CV methods, structural analyses, and supplementary ablations of time-lagging, freezing, encoder size, and conditioning placement.

The reported hybrid steering results are promising: BIOEMU-CV achieves target-hit rates of 100% on Chignolin and 93.8% on BBA, compared with at most 43.8% and 18.8% for the competing learned CVs under that protocol.
weaknesses: The principal steering results do not isolate the learned CV's contribution. Appendix B.4 combines every CV with target RMSD, while Table 15 shows that BIOEMU-CV alone achieves only 0–6.2% target hits on Chignolin and 0% on Trp-cage and BBA at the tested settings. Without an RMSD-only baseline, the improvement over conventional target-directed steering remains unknown. Endpoint accuracy also does not establish that the paths reproduce physical transition dynamics.

The folding free-energy comparison lacks a common physical state definition. Each method splits its own CV range into folded and unfolded basins, producing different reference quantities for the same protein. For example, Trp-cage reference free energies range from -1.45 for TAE to 4.15 kJ/mol for BIOEMU-CV. These errors therefore measure agreement for different partitions. Common structural basin definitions and shared reweighted observables are needed to establish comparable thermodynamic accuracy.

The statistical treatment weakens the OPES evidence. Appendix B.3 removes the run farthest from the mean among just four simulations, although trapping is itself an important sampling failure. Table 1 reports the absolute error of the mean estimate, which can conceal cancellation between inaccurate runs. Uncertainty remains large, and BIOEMU-CV's BBA free-energy error is still 7.22 kJ/mol. All-run results and uncertainty on comparative performance are needed.

The evidence for the proposed slow-dynamics mechanism is mixed. The VAMP and committor analyses do not establish consistent superiority over existing CVs. Moreover, Table 13 shows better PMF MAE without time-lagging: 1.41 versus 3.07, despite the accompanying claim of improvement on both downstream tasks. Lag sensitivity and independent kinetic validation would strengthen the assertion that the objective specifically extracts the relevant slow modes.

The foundation model's added value and the breadth of the contribution remain insufficiently established. There is no matched protein-level generative baseline trained without BioEmu pretraining; unfreezing pretrained weights does not isolate this benefit. Three short proteins, largely shared baseline hyperparameters, and limited linear-baseline experiments provide insufficient support for broad scalability and comprehensive-benchmark claims.

Reproducibility has material gaps. The physical training lag, construction of lagged pairs from randomly sampled frames, conditioning-MLP architecture, and optimization settings are not adequately specified. The reproducibility statement ends with an unfinished code-release sentence. The target-hit definition is also inconsistent: Section 4.2 states a 2 Å cutoff, whereas Figure 4 specifies 2.5 Å for BBA.

strengths: The method offers a promising integration of time-lagged representation learning with a frozen protein diffusion model, while retaining a compact CV encoder for simulation.
The evaluation includes substantial explicit-solvent simulations on three proteins, two downstream tasks, and comparisons with established learned CV methods.

Under the combined CV/RMSD steering protocol, BioEmu-CV achieves strong target-hit rates on Chignolin and BBA. Structural analyses and appendices provide useful ablations, including disclosure of unsuccessful settings.
weaknesses: The strongest steering results depend on an additional target-RMSD coordinate (Appendix B.4). Without it, BioEmu-CV achieves only 0–6.2% target hits on Chignolin and 0% on Trp-cage and BBA (Table 15). An RMSD-only baseline is missing, leaving the learned CV's contribution to the successful hybrid protocol unresolved.

The free-energy comparison lacks common physical state definitions. Dividing each learned CV's range in half produces method-dependent folded/unfolded basins and different reference free energies; for Trp-cage, these even differ in sign (Table 1). These quantities cannot be directly compared as estimates of the same folding free-energy difference. Common structural basin definitions and observables are needed.

OPES reliability is insufficiently established. One of four runs is removed for Trp-cage and BBA based on its final result, excluding failures that matter when evaluating sampling effectiveness. Computing the absolute error after averaging free energies also permits cancellation across runs. Variances remain substantial, and BioEmu-CV's BBA free-energy error is still 7.22 kJ/mol.

The evidence does not consistently establish the claimed advantage of time-lagged conditioning. Removing the lag improves Chignolin PMF MAE from 3.07 to 1.41 (Table 13), despite the accompanying claim of improvement on both tasks. Committor correlations and VAMP scores likewise show no consistent superiority. Lag sensitivity and controls isolating BioEmu pretraining would strengthen the central explanation.

The benchmark supports a narrow setting: three miniproteins with separate training using samples from long reference trajectories. Simple PCA/TICA comparisons are limited to Trp-cage, and relevant physical CV and modern predictive/information-bottleneck baselines are missing. Data efficiency and scaling beyond these systems remain untested.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the extensive appendix. The physical training lag, construction of time-lagged pairs from randomly sampled frames, optimizer/batch settings, and conditioning-adapter specification are insufficiently documented. Section B.2 also gives a 45-dimensional input architecture despite larger feature dimensions for other proteins, and the reproducibility statement contains no usable code link.
